region: Tropical America, from Mexico through Central America to southern Brazil, centred on the Brazilian Amazon
description: Purpleheart is a heavy, very hard tropical American hardwood from several Peltogyne species, such as P. paniculata, P. venosa, P. purpurea and P. mexicana. Its heartwood is brownish when first cut, turns a vivid purple within hours, and slowly darkens to brown over the years. Woodworkers use it for turning, inlay and marquetry, furniture, flooring, tool handles and colourful accents; it dulls cutters and can turn gummy when tools run hot.

hazards.summary: A UK dermatology report described an allergic skin rash from purpleheart in a man who also reacted to Andaman padauk. Indexing suggests patch testing was done, but we could not read the paper to confirm the results, so treat this as a reported effect.
All wood dust is classified as carcinogenic to humans, mainly linked to cancers of the nose and sinuses after long-term exposure. This applies to this wood like any other.

exposure_limits.note: Applies to wood dust generally; this species has no separate ACGIH value.

related_species_note: Purpleheart is sold under the genus name and the trade does not usually say which Peltogyne species a board came from. The only purpleheart health report found (Mehta-2007) does not give a botanical name. Its patient also reacted to Andaman padauk (Pterocarpus dalbergioides), a different genus; African padauk has its own page.
image_prompt: Photorealistic studio photograph of a freshly planed purpleheart (Peltogyne spp.) board, shot at a low three-quarter angle so the face grain fills most of the frame. Heartwood a vivid, saturated violet-purple after exposure to air, with a faint grey-brown cast where the surface was most recently cut and slightly deeper brown-purple tones toward one end where it has aged; a narrow edge of off-white sapwood sharply set off along one side. Mostly straight grain with a gently interlocked, wavy zone, fine to medium even texture with small scattered pores, and a medium to high natural luster. Soft diffused daylight from upper left, gentle falloff, neutral warm-grey seamless background, shallow depth of field with the near edge tack-sharp. No text, no logos, no hands, no tools, no finish or varnish, natural unfinished wood. Wide 1200x630 composition (1.91:1) with the board centered and margin on both sides for cropping.
image_alt: Planed board of purpleheart with vivid violet-purple heartwood and a narrow edge of off-white sapwood.
notes_internal: Names verified on WFO via the matching API and GraphQL (2026-11-08): genus Peltogyne Vogel accepted, family Fabaceae; P. paniculata Benth., P. venosa (Vahl) Benth., P. purpurea Pittier and P. mexicana Martinez accepted; P. pubescens Benth. is a synonym of P. paniculata on WFO, so it is listed in synonyms. POWO could not be checked (Cloudflare challenge). Which species dominate the trade is not verified; the description names species in the genus, not 'the main traded' ones. Common names come from FPL-Peltogyne; 'purple heart' (two words) is the user-facing spelling variant, kept for search. FPL also gives 'morado' (Panama, Venezuela) and 'tananeo' (Colombia); 'morado' is left out because it is also a trade name for Santos rosewood/pau ferro (Machaerium), a lead not checked here. The only health paper found is Mehta-2007 (PubMed, no abstract, full text closed). MeSH lists Patch Tests and a Semantic Scholar machine summary says purpleheart patch-tested positive; upgrade to level 1 if the letter confirms a positive patch test to purpleheart. HSE-WIS30 Table 2 does not list purpleheart, Peltogyne or amaranth. Schlunssen-2018, Baatjies-2023 and SENSOR-2017 do not mention it. No respiratory report was found on PubMed or Europe PMC. Peltomexicanin, a quinone methide pigment from P. mexicana heartwood (Gutierrez-Macias 2016, PMID 26861267), is not linked to any health effect in that paper, so it is not listed as a compound. The FPL color description (brown when cut, deep purple on exposure, eventually dark brown) supports the image prompt.
